claim: There are 58 human receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) divided into approximately 17 subfamilies.
source: The 58 human RTKs are divided into ~17 subfamilies, each featuring unique architectures in their extracellular domain that are specialized to bind and mediate the biological actions of distinct growth factors, cytokines and hormones such as EGF, FGF, PDGF, VEGF, IGF, insulin and NGF (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010, which provides the reference for this classification.

claim: All RTKs rely on ligand-induced dimerization or rearrangement of preformed dimers to elevate the intrinsic activity of the intracellular kinase domain.
source: Despite exhibiting major structural diversity in their ectodomains, all RTKs must rely on the universal process of ligand-induced dimerization or rearrangement of preformed dimers to elevate the intrinsic activity of the intracellular kinase domain (Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lemmon and Schlessinger, 2010.

claim: In the EGFR subfamily, receptor dimerization facilitates the formation of an asymmetric kinase dimer where a donor kinase allosterically stabilizes the active conformation of the receiver kinase.
source: In the case of EGFR subfamily, receptor dimerization facilitates the formation of an asymmetric kinase dimer, wherein a donor kinase allosterically stabilizes the active conformation of the receiver kinase (Kovacs et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kovacs et al., 2015.

claim: Other RTK subfamilies require trans-phosphorylation on regulatory tyrosines located in the activation loop (A-loop) to trigger activation.
source: Other RTK subfamilies require trans-phosphorylation on regulatory tyrosines located in the activation loop (A-loop) in order to trigger activation.
evidence: This is a general statement about RTK activation mechanisms presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the resting state, kinase domains of unphosphorylated receptor tyrosine kinases are autoinhibited through a variety of mechanisms.
source: Analysis of crystal structures of unphosphorylated receptor tyrosine kinase domains representing every RTK subfamily show that in the resting state (i.e. in the absence of extracellular ligand engagement) kinase domains are autoinhibited through a variety of mechanisms (Huse and Kuriyan, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huse and Kuriyan, 2002, and refers to crystal structure analysis.

claim: In insulin receptor, MUSK, and TRK subfamilies, kinase autoinhibition is mediated by the A-loop where the conserved DFG motif blocks ATP binding and a regulatory tyrosine acts as a pseudo substrate.
source: In the case of insulin receptor, MUSK, and TRK subfamilies, kinase autoinhibition is mediated by the A-loop itself whereby the conserved DFG motif at the N-terminal end of the A-loop blocks ATP binding and a regulatory tyrosine at the C-terminus of the A-loop acts as a pseudo substrate competing with substrate binding (Hubbard, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hubbard, 2002.

claim: In FLT3, the juxtamembrane region is involved in maintaining the autoinhibited kinase conformation along with the A-loop.
source: In another model based on the crystal structure of FLT3 (Griffith et al., 2004), the juxtamembrane region located outside the conserved kinase domain is involved in maintaining the autoinhibited kinase conformation along with the A-loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Griffith et al., 2004, and refers to crystal structure analysis.

claim: In FGFR, KIT, PDGFR, and VEGFR subfamilies, kinase autoinhibition is principally mediated by a network of hydrogen bonds in the vicinity of the kinase hinge region.
source: In the case of the FGFR, KIT, PDGFR, and VEGFR subfamilies, kinase autoinhibition is principally mediated by a network of hydrogen bonds in the vicinity of the kinase hinge region that constrains the ability of the kinase to adopt the active conformation (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2007.

claim: In FGFR kinase, an arginine at the C-terminal end of the A-loop makes a salt-bridge with the catalytic base resulting in occlusion of the enzyme's active site.
source: Additionally, in FGFR kinase an arginine at the C-terminal end of the A-loop makes a salt-bridge with the catalytic base resulting in occlusion of the enzyme's active site (Mohammadi et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mohammadi et al., 1996.

claim: All receptor tyrosine kinases adopt a common active state conformation upon A-loop tyrosine phosphorylation.
source: Despite employing different modes of autoinhibition, all receptor tyrosine kinases adopt a common active state conformation upon A-loop tyrosine phosphorylation (Hubbard and Till, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hubbard and Till, 2000.

claim: A-loop phosphorylated kinases display a salt-bridge between the phosphotyrosine and a conserved arginine residue within the A-loop that causes a dramatic structural rearrangement of the A-loop.
source: The available structures of A-loop phosphorylated kinases each display a salt-bridge between the phosphotyrosine and a conserved arginine residue within the A-loop that causes a dramatic structural rearrangement of the A-loop (Huse and Kuriyan, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huse and Kuriyan, 2002, and refers to structural data.

claim: There are over 30 different naturally occurring germline and somatic gain-of-function mutations that map to the kinase domain of the four human FGF receptors (FGFR1-FGFR4).
source: There are over 30 different naturally occurring germline and somatic gain-of-function mutations that map to the kinase domain of the four human FGF receptors (FGFR1-FGFR4) with the hinge region and A-loop representing the two most common hotspots (de Ravel et al., 2005; Kan et al., 2002; McGillivray et al., 2005; Zankl et al., 2004; Deutz-Terlouw et al., 1998; Grigelioniené et al., 2000; Mortier et al., 2000; Bellus et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The hinge region and A-loop represent the two most common hotspots for gain-of-function mutations in FGFR kinase domains.
source: There are over 30 different naturally occurring germline and somatic gain-of-function mutations that map to the kinase domain of the four human FGF receptors (FGFR1-FGFR4) with the hinge region and A-loop representing the two most common hotspots (de Ravel et al., 2005; Kan et al., 2002; McGillivray et al., 2005; Zankl et al., 2004; Deutz-Terlouw et al., 1998; Grigelioniené et al., 2000; Mortier et al., 2000; Bellus et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Activating mutations in FGFR kinase domains give rise to many forms of human congenital skeletal disorders of varying clinical severity and acquired cancers.
source: These activating mutations give rise to many forms of human congenital skeletal disorders of varying clinical severity and acquired cancers (Wilkin et al., 2001; Wilkie, 2005; Webster and Donoghue, 1997; Passos-Bueno et al., 1999; Rand et al., 2005; Chesi et al., 1997; Richelda et al., 1997; Cappellen et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The molecular brake is a network of hydrogen bonds formed by three residues that suppress the ability of FGFR kinase to attain the active conformation.
source: Indeed, structural and biochemical analyses of gain-of-function mutations mapping to the kinase hinge region led us to identify a network of hydrogen bonds formed by three residues termed the molecular brake that suppress the ability of FGFR kinase to attain the active conformation (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2007, and refers to structural and biochemical analyses.

claim: Mutation at each of the three constituents of the molecular brake disrupts the network of hydrogen bonds resulting in a profound increase in the intrinsic kinase activity of FGFRs.
source: Mutation at each of the three constituents of the molecular brake disrupts the network of hydrogen bonds resulting in a profound increase in the intrinsic kinase activity of FGFRs and a variety of human skeletal disorders and cancers.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional consequences of mutations based on the authors' previous work.

claim: Pathogenic mutations at a conserved lysine in the A-loop introduce additional hydrogen bonding or hydrophobic contacts to differentially stabilize the active conformation of the A-loop.
source: More recently, through crystallographic and solution NMR analyses of five pathogenic FGFR2 kinases at a conserved lysine in the A-loop (the second hotspot), we showed that these mutations introduce additional hydrogen bonding or hydrophobic contacts to differentially stabilize the active conformation of the A-loop (Chen et al., 2013) in a dynamic two-state equilibrium regimen.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2013, and refers to crystallographic and NMR analyses.

claim: FGFR kinase domain toggles between a conformationally rigid autoinhibited state and a conformationally flexible activated state.
source: In this model, FGFR kinase domain toggles between a conformationally rigid autoinhibited state and a conformationally flexible activated state.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their previous work.

claim: The kinase activity was found to directly correlate with the fractional population of the active state.
source: Notably, the kinase activity was found to directly correlate with the fractional population of the active state.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: In structures of A-loop mutants, the hydrogen bonds at the molecular brake, which are over 25 Å from the mutational site, were broken.
source: In all structures of A-loop mutants, the hydrogen bonds at the molecular brake, which are over 25 Å from the mutational site, were broken leading us to infer the existence of a long-range allosteric connectivity between the A-loop and molecular brake.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structures analyzed in the study.

claim: There is long-range allosteric connectivity between the A-loop and molecular brake in FGFR kinases.
source: In all structures of A-loop mutants, the hydrogen bonds at the molecular brake, which are over 25 Å from the mutational site, were broken leading us to infer the existence of a long-range allosteric connectivity between the A-loop and molecular brake.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: The DFG latch and αC tether are two clusters of hydrophobic interactions that relay allosteric signals between the A-loop and the molecular brake.
source: Our data reveal two clusters of hydrophobic interactions, termed 'DFG latch' and 'αC tether', which relay allosteric signals between the A-loop and the molecular brake.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study based on X-ray crystallography, NMR spectroscopy, and kinase assays.

claim: The DFG latch and αC tether are located strategically at the interface between the N- and C-lobes of the kinase.
source: These hydrophobic networks, located strategically at the interface between the N- and C-lobes of the kinase, sense the structural fluctuations in the A-loop and molecular brake and undergo rearrangements to determine the kinase interlobe angle and hence kinase activation.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the study.

claim: The DFG latch and αC tether sense structural fluctuations in the A-loop and molecular brake and undergo rearrangements to determine the kinase interlobe angle and hence kinase activation.
source: These hydrophobic networks, located strategically at the interface between the N- and C-lobes of the kinase, sense the structural fluctuations in the A-loop and molecular brake and undergo rearrangements to determine the kinase interlobe angle and hence kinase activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of structural and functional data from the study.

claim: Naturally occurring pathogenic and acquired drug-resistant mutations seize the four-site allosteric control pathway to bias the kinase equilibrium toward the active state.
source: Naturally occurring pathogenic and acquired drug-resistant mutations seize the four-site allosteric control pathway to bias the kinase equilibrium toward the active state thereby causing excessive signaling in human skeletal disorders and cancers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The four-site allosteric mechanism is shared by PDGFRs, KIT, VEGFRs, and CSF1R.
source: In addition to enriching our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of FGFR-related diseases, these findings are anticipated to make a major impact for ongoing drug discovery efforts targeting FGFRs and other RTKs such as PDGFRs, KIT, VEGFRs, and CSF1R that share the four-site allosteric mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural similarity.

claim: The crystal structure of K659E FGFR2K shows that the molecular brake is disengaged.
source: Overlays of crystal structures corresponding to unphosphorylated K659E FGFR2K (PDB ID: 4J97 [Chen et al., 2013], in magenta), unphosphorylated K659M FGFR2K (PDB ID: 4J96 [Chen et al., 2013], in cyan), unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K (PDB ID: 2PSQ [Chen et al., 2007], in green) and the A-loop phosphorylated WT FGFR2K (PDB ID: 2PVF [Chen et al., 2007], in grey). The insets to the left of the panel display close-up views of the molecular brake regions of each of the four superimposed crystal structures.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The K659E mutation introduces three hydrogen bonds that support the active conformation of the A-loop.
source: The three hydrogen bonds introduced by the K659E mutation that support the active conformation of the A-loop are shown as red dashed lines.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The K659M mutation introduces hydrophobic interactions that stabilize the active A-loop conformation.
source: The hydrophobic interactions introduced by the K659M mutation are represented by semitransparent surfaces, and the hydrogen bonds between Y657 and R649 are shown as red dashed lines.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The A-loop conformation of the N549H mutant is identical to that of unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K despite the dissociation of the molecular brake by the mutation.
source: Note that the A-loop conformation of the N549H mutant is identical to that of unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K despite the dissociation of the molecular brake by the mutation.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure comparison shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The orientation of the αC helix in the crystal structure of unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K is similar to those seen in crystal structures of the A-loop phosphorylated FGFR1K and FGFR2K.
source: The orientation of the αC helix (rendered as a cylinder) in the crystal structure of unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K is similar to those seen in crystal structures of the A-loop phosphorylated FGFR1K and FGFR2K.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure comparison shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The conformation of first seven residues of the A-loop (DFGLARD) of the unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K resembles those of phosphorylated activated FGFR1K and FGFR2K.
source: The conformation of first seven residues of the A-loop (DFGLARD) of the unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K resembles those of phosphorylated activated FGFR1K and FGFR2K.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure comparison shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The unphosphorylated FGFR2K features the β9 strand which pairs with the catalytic loop, similar to phosphorylated activated FGFRK structures.
source: Note that as in these latter phosphorylated activated FGFRK structures, the unphosphorylated FGFR2K features the β9 strand which pairs with the catalytic loop.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure comparison shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In unphosphorylated FGFR1K and FGFR4K, a salt-bridge between an FGFR-invariant arginine and the catalytic base blocks the active site.
source: The substrate tyrosine binding site in the unphosphorylated FGFR2K is fully accessible which is in stark contrast to that in the unphosphorylated FGFR1K and FGFR4K in which a prominent salt-bridge between an FGFR-invariant arginine (R661 in FGFR1K, R664 in FGFR2K and R655 in FGFR4K) and the catalytic base (D623 in FGFR1K, D626 in FGFR2K and D617 in FGFR4K) blocks the active site.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure comparison shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The substrate tyrosine binding site in the unphosphorylated FGFR2K is fully accessible.
source: The substrate tyrosine binding site in the unphosphorylated FGFR2K is fully accessible which is in stark contrast to that in the unphosphorylated FGFR1K and FGFR4K in which a prominent salt-bridge between an FGFR-invariant arginine (R661 in FGFR1K, R664 in FGFR2K and R655 in FGFR4K) and the catalytic base (D623 in FGFR1K, D626 in FGFR2K and D617 in FGFR4K) blocks the active site.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A tightly bound sulfate ion in the crystal structures of unphosphorylated FGFR2K occupies a similar location as the phosphate moiety of the phosphorylated A-loop tyrosine 657 in the phosphorylated active FGFR2K structure.
source: Notably in the crystal structures of the unphosphorylated FGFR2K (2PSQ) and its molecular brake mutants (2Q0B, 2PWL, 2PZ5, 2PY3, 2PZR), a tightly bound sulfate ion occupies a similar location as the phosphate moiety of the phosphorylated A-loop tyrosine 657 (pTyr-657) in the phosphorylated active FGFR2K structure.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structure analysis.

claim: The sulfate ion in unphosphorylated FGFR2K structures makes hydrogen bonds with the invariant arginine from the DFGLARD motif reminiscent of pTyr-657 in the phosphorylated active FGFR2K.
source: This sulfate ion makes hydrogen bonds with the invariant arginine from the DFGLARD motif reminiscent of pTyr-657 in the phosphorylated active FGFR2K.
evidence: This is an observation from crystal structure analysis.

claim: The partially active kinase conformation seen in the crystal structures of the unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K and its molecular brake mutants have been influenced by crystal packing and the presence of the sulfate ion.
source: Hence, it appears that the partially active kinase conformation seen in the crystal structures of the unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K (2PSQ) and its molecular brake mutants have been influenced by crystal packing and the presence of the sulfate ion trapped in the A-loop.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: Chemical shift perturbations between unphosphorylated and monophosphorylated FGFR2K show significant perturbations for several residues in the C-lobe.
source: Plotting of the chemical shift differences between the unphosphorylated and monophosphorylated (pY657) activated FGFR2K onto the crystal structures of unphosphorylated FGFR1K (3KY2) and FGFR2K (2PSQ) shows significant perturbations for several residues in the C-lobe including the αEF helix (L675), αF helix (V691), and αG helix (I707, V709, E711, L712, F713, K717, E718, and M722) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on NMR chemical shift mapping analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PRE experiments show that Y656 and Y657 in FGFR2K are approximately 19 Å away from the MTSL-labeled C707.
source: Both Y656 and Y657 were found to be ~19 Å away from the MTSL-labeled C707, which is in better agreement with the A-loop conformation in the FGFR1K structure (3KY2) than the A-loop conformation in FGFR2K (2PSQ).
evidence: This is based on PRE NMR experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The A-loop conformation in the unphosphorylated FGFR2K structure (2PSQ) is not a genuinely inhibited conformation.
source: Hence, as with the chemical shift data, our PRE results also imply that the A-loop conformation in the unphosphorylated FGFR2K structure (2PSQ) is not a genuinely inhibited conformation, and that in solution the A-loop of FGFR2K most likely adopts a similar conformation as that displayed by the A-loops of unphosphorylated FGFR1K (3KY2) and FGFR4K (4QQT) in the crystal.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on NMR data (chemical shift and PRE experiments).

claim: The crystal structure of the FGFR2KE565A/N549H double mutant shows a disengaged molecular brake.
source: Similar to crystal structures of single mutants of the molecular brake, the FGFR2KE565A/N549H structure showed a disengaged molecular brake (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The A-loop in the FGFR2KE565A/N549H structure adopted a catalytically active conformation with striking resemblance to that of A-loop phosphorylated FGFR2K.
source: However, unlike these previous structures the A-loop in the FGFR2KE565A/N549H structure adopted a catalytically active conformation with striking resemblance to that of A-loop phosphorylated FGFR2K (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The DFG latch is a cluster of hydrophobic interactions centering on the phenylalanine from the RTK-invariant DFG motif.
source: Analysis of the I547V and L617M/F mutations in the context of autoinhibited and activated FGFRK crystal structures revealed a previously unrecognized cluster of hydrophobic interactions centering on the phenylalanine from the RTK-invariant DFG motif (Figure 4C,E and G). This hydrophobic cluster, which we have termed the DFG latch, determines the conformation of the N-terminal part of the A-loop and hence the N-lobe rotation.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of pathogenic mutations shown in Figure 4.

claim: The DFG latch determines the conformation of the N-terminal part of the A-loop and hence the N-lobe rotation.
source: This hydrophobic cluster, which we have termed the DFG latch, determines the conformation of the N-terminal part of the A-loop and hence the N-lobe rotation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of structural data.

claim: In autoinhibited FGFR kinases, the conformations of the DFG and adjacent LAR residues are physically incompatible with downward rotation of the αC helix toward the C-lobe.
source: Specifically, in the autoinhibited FGFR1K, FGFR3K, and FGFR4K structures, the conformations of the DFG and adjacent LAR residues are physically incompatible with downward rotation of the αC helix toward the C-lobe, a well-documented mandatory event in kinase activation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In autoinhibited FGFR kinases, the phenylalanine of the DFG motif is fixed in its inhibitory position through tight hydrophobic interactions with L617, I553, and I541.
source: The inhibited conformation of the DFGLAR motif is primarily dictated by the DFG latch where the phenylalanine is fixed in its observed inhibitory position through tight hydrophobic interactions with L617 from the αE helix, I553 from the αC-β4 loop, and I541 from the αC helix of FGFR2K (Figure 4C,E and G).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4C, E, and G.

claim: In phosphorylated activated FGFRK structures, a salt bridge between the arginine within the DFGLAR motif and the phosphotyrosine in the A-loop is formed.
source: In the phosphorylated activated FGFRK structures, however, an RTK-invariant salt bridge between the arginine within the DFGLAR motif and the phosphotyrosine in the A-loop is formed.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The intraloop salt bridge in activated kinases facilitates backbone hydrogen bonding between the arginine and the conserved I623 resulting in the formation of the short β6-β9 sheet.
source: This intraloop salt bridge facilitates backbone hydrogen bonding between this same arginine and the conserved I623 situated in the catalytic loop resulting in the formation of the short β6-β9 sheet (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In activated kinases, the χ1 side chain dihedral angle of F645 rotates by 120° placing the side chain in a new location conducive with downward rotation of the N-lobe.
source: This structural change alters the conformation of the preceding DFG latch causing the χ1 side chain dihedral angle of F645 to rotate by 120° which places the side chain of F645 in a new location that is now conducive with downward rotation of the N-lobe (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In activated kinases, the hydrophobic DFG latch becomes less engaged relative to the autoinhibited kinase as indicated by longer distances between the phenylalanine and the other three constituents of the latch.
source: Notably, in the activated kinase, the hydrophobic DFG latch becomes less engaged relative to the autoinhibited kinase as indicated by longer distances between the phenylalanine and the other three constituents of the latch (I541, I547, L617) as well as a decrease in shape complementarity (Figure 4D,F and I).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4D, F, and I.

claim: The L617M/F and I547V gain-of-function mutations act by weakening the DFG latch that encourages the movement of the N-lobe toward the C-lobe.
source: According to this structural analysis, the L617M/F and I547V gain-of-function mutations act by weakening the DFG latch that encourages the movement of the N-lobe toward the C-lobe, which under physiological conditions would be accomplished by A-loop tyrosine phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of structural data.

claim: The weakened hydrophobic contact between F645 of the DFG motif and I547 perturbs the hydrogen bonding network at the molecular brake resulting in its disengagement.
source: In addition, we postulate that the weakened hydrophobic contact between F645 of the DFG motif and I547, which is situated on the same αC-β4 loop as N549, perturbs the hydrogen bonding network at the molecular brake resulting in its disengagement.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claim: The DFG conformation in activated FGFRK structures is distinct from the 'DFG-out' conformation induced by type II ATP competitive inhibitors.
source: It should be noted that the DFG conformation seen in the activated FGFRK structures is distinct from the so-called 'DFG-out' conformation induced by binding of type II ATP competitive inhibitors such as Ponatinib and Gleevec (Schindler et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a clarification based on comparison with known inhibitor-bound structures, supported by a citation.

claim: In autoinhibited FGFRK structures, the conserved aspartic acid (D650 in FGFR2K) does not play any role in stabilizing the autoinhibited conformation of the A-loop.
source: In autoinhibited FGFRK structures, the conserved aspartic acid (D650 in FGFR2K) does not play any role in stabilizing the autoinhibited conformation of the A-loop (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In activated kinase structures, D650 makes van der Waals contacts with two conserved methionines (M537 and M540) at the C-terminal end of the αC helix.
source: However, in activated kinase structures, it makes van der Waals contacts with two conserved methionines (M537 and M540 in FGFR2K) at the C-terminal end of the αC helix (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The van der Waals contacts between D650 and M537/M540 cooperate with the arginine-phosphotyrosine salt bridge to further promote β9-β6 strand formation.
source: These van der Waals/hydrophobic contacts cooperate with the aforementioned arginine-phosphotyrosine salt bridge to further promote the β9-β6 strand formation (Figure 5C), thus encouraging movement of the phenylalanine from the DFG motif to facilitate N-lobe rotation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of structural data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: D650V or M537I mutations in FGFR2K may accentuate the hydrophobic contacts between the A-loop and the αC helix to facilitate N-lobe rotation and kinase activation.
source: Based on this structural analysis, D650V or M537I mutations in FGFR2K may accentuate the hydrophobic contacts between the A-loop and the aαC helix to facilitate N-lobe rotation and hence kinase activation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on structural analysis.

claim: Phosphorylation on the A-loop tyrosine triggers a series of concerted allosteric motions to couple all four sites thereby conferring catalytic competency on FGFRKs.
source: Thus, according to our four-site allosteric model, phosphorylation on the A-loop tyrosine triggers a series of concerted allosteric motions to couple all four sites thereby conferring catalytic competency on FGFRKs (see model in Figure 6).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on their structural and functional data, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: All the DFG latch mutants (I547V, L617M, L617F, L617V) exhibited elevated kinase activity compared to WT FGFR2K.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, all the mutants exhibited elevated kinase activity compared to WT, which supports our hypothesis that the DFG latch suppresses FGFRK activity.
evidence: This is based on in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The DFG latch suppresses FGFRK activity.
source: As shown in Figure 7A, all the mutants exhibited elevated kinase activity compared to WT, which supports our hypothesis that the DFG latch suppresses FGFRK activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on kinase assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The I547V mutation in FGFR2K and its analogous I538V mutation in FGFR3K lead to gain-of-function and cause skeletal disorders and cancer.
source: The fact that both I547V mutation in FGFR2K and its analogous I538V mutation in FGFR3K lead to gain-of-function and cause skeletal disorders and cancer (Pollock et al., 2007; Grigelioniené et al., 1998) strongly suggests that the DFG latch is applicable to all four FGFR isoforms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The DFG latch is applicable to all four FGFR isoforms.
source: The fact that both I547V mutation in FGFR2K and its analogous I538V mutation in FGFR3K lead to gain-of-function and cause skeletal disorders and cancer (Pollock et al., 2007; Grigelioniené et al., 1998) strongly suggests that the DFG latch is applicable to all four FGFR isoforms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of the mutation effect across FGFR isoforms.

claim: Mutations of the corresponding isoleucine and leucine residues of the DFG latch in FGFR1K caused activation.
source: Indeed, mutations of the corresponding isoleucine and leucine residues of the DFG latch in FGFR1K also caused activation (Figure 7A inset).
evidence: This is based on kinase assay data shown in Figure 7A inset.

claim: FGFR2K mutants that strengthen the αC tether (D650A, D650L, D650V, D650I, M537I) were 3- to 19-fold more active than unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K.
source: Relative to the unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K, the D650A, D650L, D650V, D650I, and M537I mutants were 3- to 19-fold more active (Figure 7B), whereas the D650G, M537A, and M540A mutants were less active (Figure 7B inset).
evidence: This is based on kinase assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: FGFR2K mutants that weaken the αC tether (D650G, M537A, M540A) were less active than unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K.
source: Relative to the unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K, the D650A, D650L, D650V, D650I, and M537I mutants were 3- to 19-fold more active (Figure 7B), whereas the D650G, M537A, and M540A mutants were less active (Figure 7B inset).
evidence: This is based on kinase assay data shown in Figure 7B inset.

claim: The αC tether regulates FGFRK activity.
source: These data provide strong support for the role of the αC tether in regulating FGFRK activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on kinase assay data.

claim: The D650V FGFR2K mutant crystallized in a fully activated conformation displaying a disengaged molecular brake and an activated A-loop conformation.
source: Consistent with our prediction, D650V crystallized in a fully activated conformation displaying a disengaged molecular brake and an activated A-loop conformation (Figure 8A,D and E).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: In the D650V mutant structure, the mutated V650 residue makes strong hydrophobic contacts with M537 and M540 between the αC helix and the A-loop.
source: Additional structural analysis showed that the mutated V650 residue makes strong hydrophobic contacts with M537 and M540 between the αC helix and the A-loop thereby facilitating the rotation of the αC helix toward the C-lobe (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: In the D650V mutant structure, the DFG latch is rearranged in a non-inhibitory conformation to facilitate N-lobe rotation.
source: As expected, the DFG latch is rearranged in a non-inhibitory conformation to facilitate N-lobe rotation (Figure 8B), which in turn leads to the disengagement of the molecular brake (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Mutations targeting one of the allosteric sites influence the chemical environment of distal sites.
source: Taken together, these backbone chemical shift data show that mutations targeting one of the allosteric sites influence the chemical environment of distal sites and therefore support our proposed four-site long-range allosteric network.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on NMR chemical shift perturbation data.

claim: Mutation at the DFG latch (I547V) caused chemical shift perturbations for residues within the molecular brake, αC tether, and catalytic loop.
source: Mutation at the DFG latch (I547V) caused chemical shift perturbations for residues within the molecular brake, αC tether, and catalytic loop (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is based on NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Mutations affecting the αC tether (M537I, D650V) gave chemical shift changes to G646 of the DFG motif and I623 from the catalytic loop.
source: Likewise, mutations affecting the αC tether (M537I, D650V) gave small but significant chemical shift changes to G646 of the DFG motif and I623 from the catalytic loop.
evidence: This is based on NMR chemical shift perturbation data.

claim: The D650V mutation induced a perturbation at A567, which is in the vicinity of the molecular brake.
source: Notably, the D650V mutation induced a perturbation at A567, which is in the vicinity of the molecular brake, whereas the M537I mutation did not significantly perturb this residue.
evidence: This is based on NMR chemical shift perturbation data.

claim: Mutations at the molecular brake (N549T, E565A, K641R) induced significant chemical shift changes to residues at or proximal to the molecular brake, DFG latch, αC tether, and catalytic loop.
source: Finally, mutations at the molecular brake (N549T, E565A, K641R) induced significant chemical shift changes to residues at or proximal to the molecular brake, DFG latch, αC tether, and catalytic loop (Figure 9A; Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on NMR chemical shift perturbation data shown in Figure 9A and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The E565A mutant incurred major chemical shift changes at residues both proximal to the molecular brake and distal from the molecular brake at the DFG motif and A-loop.
source: The E565A mutant incurred major chemical shift changes at residues both proximal to the molecular brake (I548, L551, V564) and distal from the molecular brake at the DFG motif (I541, I547) and A-loop (L647, I651).
evidence: This is based on NMR methyl group chemical shift perturbation data.

claim: Disruption of the hydrogen bonding network of the molecular brake influences the conformation of the A-loop via long-range allostery.
source: These data demonstrate that disruption of the hydrogen bonding network of the molecular brake influences the conformation of the A-loop via long-range allostery.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on NMR chemical shift perturbation data.

claim: Several residues in the K659E mutant showed significant relaxation dispersions at the backbone amide and side chain methyl groups.
source: Indeed, several residues in the K659E mutant showed significant relaxation dispersions (i.e. ΔR2,eff >2 s−1) both at the backbone amide and side chain methyl groups (Figure 10C–F).
evidence: This is based on CPMG relaxation dispersion NMR experiments shown in Figure 10C-F.

claim: The K659E mutant interconverts between the autoinhibited/active states on a µsec-msec timescale with an exchange rate (kex) of 2000 ± 500 s−1.
source: Based on this analysis, an exchange rate (kex) of 2000 ± 500 s−1 was estimated (Figure 10F) indicating that this pathogenic mutant interconverts between the autoinhibited/active states on a µsec-msec timescale (i.e. fast-intermediate exchange).
evidence: This is based on analysis of CPMG relaxation dispersion data shown in Figure 10F.

claim: Unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K showed very few residues exhibiting relaxation dispersions.
source: By contrast, CPMG relaxation dispersion measurements on unphosphorylated WT FGFR2K showed very few residues exhibiting relaxation dispersions (Figure 10A and B).
evidence: This is based on CPMG relaxation dispersion NMR experiments shown in Figure 10A and B.

claim: The unphosphorylated form of FGFR2K is conformationally rigid with only a small fraction of kinase molecules in the active state conformation.
source: Based on these observations, we conclude that the unphosphorylated form of FGFR2K is conformationally rigid (i.e. only a small fraction of kinase molecules are in the active state conformation).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on CPMG relaxation dispersion NMR data.

claim: The kinase domain of FGFR is subject to a three-level autoinhibition mechanism via the molecular brake, the DFG latch and the blockade of the active site by the A-loop/catalytic loop salt bridge (A-loop plug).
source: These NMR data are congruent with the X-ray crystal structures showing that the kinase domain of FGFR is subject to a three-level autoinhibition mechanism via the molecular brake, the DFG latch and the blockade of the active site by the A-loop/catalytic loop salt bridge (A-loop plug).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on integration of NMR and X-ray crystallography data.

claim: Comparison of spectra between unphosphorylated and monophosphorylated activated FGFR2K showed a substantial reduction in peak intensities for the DFG motif and catalytic loop in the monophosphorylated activated FGFR2K.
source: Comparison of these spectra with those of unphosphorylated (inhibited) WT FGFR2K showed a substantial reduction in peak intensities for the DFG motif and catalytic loop in the monophosphorylated activated FGFR2K.
evidence: This is based on NMR spectral comparison.

claim: The DFG motif in the autoinhibited kinase is conformationally rigid, whereas in the active form it becomes mobile with conformational fluctuations occurring on the µsec-msec timescale.
source: These observations reiterate that the DFG motif in the autoinhibited kinase is conformationally rigid (i.e. DFG latch on), whereas in the active form it becomes mobile with conformational fluctuations occurring on the µsec-msec timescale.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on NMR data.

claim: CPMG relaxation dispersions experiments on K659E showed significant relaxation dispersions for F645 and the surrounding methyl groups of I541 and I547.
source: Notably, CPMG relaxation dispersions experiments performed on K659E also showed significant relaxation dispersions for F645 and the surrounding methyl groups of I541 and I547.
evidence: This is based on CPMG relaxation dispersion NMR experiments.

claim: Kinase activation by A-loop phosphorylation or by pathogenic mutations enhances conformational dynamics of the enzyme and leads to a weakening of the DFG latch.
source: These data further support that kinase activation by A-loop phosphorylation or by pathogenic mutations enhances conformational dynamics of the enzyme and leads to a weakening of the DFG latch consistent with our structural analysis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on NMR data and structural analysis.

claim: Enhanced conformational dynamics on the µsec-msec timescale for the DFG motif upon activation might be a general feature of all protein kinases.
source: Our data are consistent with the previously published NMR data for other activated protein kinases including protein kinase A (Masterson et al., 2008) and p38 MAP kinase (Vogtherr et al., 2006), which also showed broadening around the DFG motif. Hence, it appears that enhanced conformational dynamics on the µsec-msec timescale for the DFG motif upon activation might be a general feature of all protein kinases.
evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison with published data for other kinases, supported by citations.

claim: CHESCA analysis identified 18 residues that comprise the same allosteric network.
source: In total, 18 residues were found to comprise the same allosteric network shown in Figure 9C and D.
evidence: This is based on CHESCA analysis shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: CHESCA analysis identified allosterically coupled residues belonging to the catalytic loop, region surrounding the molecular brake, αF helix, Gly-rich loop, and A-loop.
source: Mapping these sites onto the autoinhibited FGFR1K structure (PDB ID: 3KY2) illuminated a network of allosterically coupled residues belonging to the catalytic loop (D626 to N631), region surrounding the molecular brake (T635), αF helix (F689), Gly-rich loop (G488, F492), and A-loop (A643).
evidence: This is based on CHESCA analysis.

claim: The identification of A643 by CHESCA is harmonious with the crystallographically deduced role of the DFG latch as a conduit in the allostery transmission from the A-loop to the molecular brake.
source: The identification of A643, which is located immediately before D644 of the DFG motif, is harmonious with the crystallographically deduced role of the DFG latch as a conduit in the allostery transmission from the A-loop to the molecular brake.
evidence: This is an interpretation that integrates CHESCA results with structural data.

claim: The identification of D626 and other catalytic loop residues by CHESCA strongly supports a major conformational change of the A-loop between the inhibited and activated structures.
source: Likewise the identification of D626 and other catalytic loop residues by CHESCA strongly supports a major conformational change of the A-loop between the inhibited and activated structures, which is induced by A-loop tyrosine phosphorylation and mimicked by pathogenic mutations.
evidence: This is an interpretation that integrates CHESCA results with structural knowledge.

claim: In autoinhibited FGFRK structures, D623 engages in a salt bridge with R661 from the A-loop thereby blocking the substrate-binding site.
source: As mentioned earlier, in the autoinhibited FGFRK structures (e.g., FGFR1K, PDB ID: 3KY2), D623 in FGFR1K corresponding to D626 in FGFR2K engages in a salt bridge with R661 from the A-loop thereby blocking the substrate-binding site (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Upon activation, the arginine residue disengages from the aspartate and makes a cation-Π interaction with the incoming substrate tyrosine.
source: Upon activation this arginine residue disengages from the aspartate and makes a cation-Π interaction with the incoming substrate tyrosine (Huang et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: ATP binding alone is ineffective in altering the hydrogen bonding network of the molecular brake or switching the phenylalanine position in the DFG latch.
source: However, a direct comparison of the crystal structures of inhibited and activated kinases in complex with AMP-PCP (Mohammadi et al., 1996b), a nonhydrolyzable ATP analog, clearly shows that ATP binding alone is ineffective in altering the hydrogen bonding network of the molecular brake or switching the phenylalanine position in the DFG latch.
evidence: This is based on comparison of crystal structures with ATP analog bound.

claim: Despite binding the ATP analog, unphosphorylated FGFRK remains in the inhibited conformation.
source: In other words, despite binding the ATP analog, unphosphorylated FGFRK remains in the inhibited conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural analysis.

claim: Only the adenosine portion of the ATP analog is ordered in the crystal structure of unphosphorylated kinase.
source: Notably, in contrast to the fully ordered ATP analog in the crystal structure of the phosphorylated kinase-ATP complex, only the adenosine portion of the ATP analog is ordered in the crystal structure of unphosphorylated kinase (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The DFG conformation for the unphosphorylated kinase is not permissive for Mg2+ ion coordination by the conserved aspartic acid resulting in a disordered state of the phosphate moieties within the ATP analog.
source: This is due to the fact that the DFG conformation for the unphosphorylated kinase is not permissive for Mg2+ ion coordination by the conserved aspartic acid resulting in a disordered state of the phosphate moieties within the ATP analog.
evidence: This is an interpretation of structural data.

claim: Compared to pathogenic mutations that directly target the four regions of the allosteric network, ATP is a poor extrinsic effector of conformational equilibrium between the active and inhibited states.
source: Therefore, compared to pathogenic mutations that directly target the four regions of the allosteric network, ATP is a poor extrinsic effector of conformational equilibrium between the active and inhibited states.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural and NMR data.

claim: Addition of AMP-PCP induced large chemical shift changes for residues in the proximity of the ATP binding pocket but most C-lobe residues were insensitive to the presence of AMP-PCP.
source: As expected, addition of AMP-PCP induced large chemical shift changes for residues in the proximity of the ATP binding pocket including the 'gatekeeper' residue (V564) and glycine-rich loop residues (i.e. G488, G490). By contrast, most C-lobe residues including residues V691 and L712, that tether A-loop tyrosine to the C-lobe, were completely insensitive to the presence of AMP-PCP or experienced only minor perturbations (i.e. L675) implying that nucleotide binding does not significantly impact the A-loop conformation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on NMR chemical shift perturbation experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AMP-PCP (mimic of ATP) binding to an autoinhibited enzyme cannot force the A-loop to the active conformation.
source: Hence, in agreement with X-ray data, the NMR results also demonstrate that AMP-PCP (mimic of ATP) binding to an autoinhibited enzyme cannot force the A-loop to the active conformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on NMR data that agrees with X-ray data.

claim: ATP is unlikely to serve as a physiological means in modulating intrinsic dynamics of the FGFRK.
source: Furthermore, given that ATP concentration in the cytosol is relatively constant between 1 and 10 mM, ATP is unlikely to serve as a physiological means in modulating intrinsic dynamics of the FGFRK.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the constant ATP concentration in cells and the experimental findings.

claim: None of the FGFR2K pathogenic mutants are capable of achieving the activity exerted by A-loop phosphorylation.
source: The kinase activity data establish that none of the FGFR2K pathogenic mutants are capable of achieving the activity exerted by A-loop phosphorylation (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on kinase activity measurements shown in Figure 7.

claim: Pathogenic mutations only partially mimic the active kinase conformation achieved by A-loop phosphorylation.
source: Consistent with these activity measurements, NMR data show that the pathogenic mutations only partially mimic the active kinase conformation achieved by A-loop phosphorylation (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on NMR data, supported by a citation.

claim: The E565A mutant showed the largest signal attenuations for backbone amide and methyl group resonances around the DFG motif.
source: The E565A mutant showed the largest signal attenuations for backbone amide and methyl group resonances where notable reductions in peak heights were seen around the DFG motif albeit to a lesser extent than that for A-loop phosphorylated FGFR2K (Figure 11).
evidence: This is based on NMR spectral analysis shown in Figure 11.

claim: The E565A mutant possesses the greatest intrinsic activity among the FGFR2K mutants studied.
source: This observation is consistent with the fact that the E565A mutant possesses the greatest intrinsic activity among the FGFR2K mutants studied.
evidence: This is based on kinase activity measurements.

claim: Three out of the four sites of the allosteric network (molecular brake, DFG latch, A-loop plug) mediate strong hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic intramolecular contacts that repress the kinase from adopting an active conformation.
source: Specifically, three out of the four sites of the allosteric network (molecular brake, DFG latch, A-loop plug) mediate strong hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic intramolecular contacts that repress the kinase from adopting an active conformation.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claim: Only the αC tether site provides van der Waals forces to encourage the active conformation.
source: Only the αC tether site provides van der Waals forces to encourage the active conformation.
evidence: This is a summary of the structural findings.

claim: Evolution of the FGFR kinase structure has favored a biased design to impose tight autoinhibition on the kinase.
source: Thus, evolution of the FGFR kinase structure has favored a biased design to impose tight autoinhibition on the kinase that severely limits the ability of the enzyme to adopt the active state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural and functional data.

claim: Mutational derepression of only one of the three autoinhibitory sites or mutational strengthening of the αC tether alone does not completely convert the kinase to the active state.
source: Consequently, mutational derepression of only one of the three autoinhibitory sites (molecular brake, DFG latch or A-loop plug) or mutational strengthening of the αC tether alone does not completely convert the kinase to the active state, which implies that mutation in one site partially accesses the conformation of the remaining three sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on kinase activity and structural data.

claim: A-loop phosphorylation and the subsequent formation of an intra-loop pTyr-Arg salt bridge is the most effective way to fully couple the four sites to give rise to the largest fraction of activated kinase population.
source: In other words, A-loop phosphorylation and the subsequent formation of an intra-loop pTyr-Arg salt bridge is the most effective way to fully couple the four sites to give rise to the largest fraction of activated kinase population.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on kinase activity and structural data.

claim: The differential abilities of pathogenic mutations to couple all four sites translate into differences in active state populations which correlate with the gradations in gain-of-function and the associated clinical severity found in skeletal syndromes.
source: Notably, the differential abilities of pathogenic mutations to couple all four sites translate into differences in active state populations for these mutations which correlate with the gradations in gain-of-function and the associated clinical severity found in skeletal syndromes caused by the mutations (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings, supported by a citation.

claim: The activities of all double mutants targeting different allosteric regions were higher than the individual mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 12A, the activities of all double mutants targeting different allosteric regions were higher than the individual mutants.
evidence: This is based on kinase activity measurements shown in Figure 12A.

claim: The activity of the E565A/K659M double mutant nearly reached the maximal activity achieved by A-loop phosphorylated WT FGFR2K.
source: In fact, the activity of the E565A/K659M double mutant nearly reached the maximal activity achieved by A-loop phosphorylated WT FGFR2K.
evidence: This is based on kinase activity measurements.

claim: The D650V/M537I mutant was more active than either of the D650V and M537I single mutants as well as their added activities, but was unable to reach the activity of the A-loop phosphorylated WT kinase.
source: The D650V/M537I mutant was more active than either of the D650V and M537I single mutants as well as their added activities, but was unable to reach the activity of the A-loop phosphorylated WT kinase.
evidence: This is based on kinase activity measurements.

claim: Double mutants targeting the same allosteric site (N549H/E565A) or two adjoining sites (I547V/E565A) gave only a subtle increase in activity beyond those of the single mutants.
source: By contrast, double mutants targeting the same allosteric site (N549H/E565A) or two adjoining sites (I547V/E565A) gave only a subtle increase in activity beyond those of the single mutants.
evidence: This is based on kinase activity measurements.

claim: The lack of synergy between N549H and E565A mutations in elevating kinase activity is expected as either mutation alone is sufficient to disrupt the hydrogen bonding network at the molecular brake.
source: This lack of synergy between N549H and E565A mutations in elevating kinase activity is expected as either mutation alone is sufficient to disrupt the hydrogen bonding network at the molecular brake.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the kinase activity data.

claim: Double mutations among the four sites of the allosteric network can reinforce each other in increasing the enzymatic activity.
source: These extensive kinase assay data show that double mutations among the four sites of the allosteric network can reinforce each other in increasing the enzymatic activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on kinase activity measurements.

claim: A rare case of Thanatophoric Dysplasia is caused by double missense FGFR3 mutations in cis (N540K and V555M) located in the molecular brake and near the DFG latch.
source: The physiological evidence for synergism between gain-of-function mutations is provided by a recent discovery of a rare case of Thanatophoric Dysplasia (TD) caused by double missense FGFR3 mutations in cis (N540K and V555M) located in the molecular brake and near the DFG latch (Pannier et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The N540K mutation accounts for 70% of Hypochondroplasia cases and results in a mild form of dwarfism.
source: While the N540K mutation accounts for 70% of Hypochondroplasia cases and results in a mild form of dwarfism, the combination of this mutation with V555M results in TD, a neonatal lethal skeletal syndrome, presumably due to greater gain-of-function of the double mutant relative to the single mutations alone.
evidence: This is a statement about the clinical phenotype associated with the mutation.

claim: The combination of N540K with V555M results in Thanatophoric Dysplasia, a neonatal lethal skeletal syndrome, presumably due to greater gain-of-function of the double mutant relative to the single mutations alone.
source: While the N540K mutation accounts for 70% of Hypochondroplasia cases and results in a mild form of dwarfism, the combination of this mutation with V555M results in TD, a neonatal lethal skeletal syndrome, presumably due to greater gain-of-function of the double mutant relative to the single mutations alone.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism based on the clinical phenotype.

claim: Both double mutants (E565A/K659M and E565A/D650V) crystallized in an activated conformation displaying an active A-loop conformation, a disengaged molecular brake, a weakened DFG latch and an engaged αC tether.
source: In agreement with their elevated kinase activities, both double mutants crystallized in an activated conformation displaying an active A-loop conformation, a disengaged molecular brake, a weakened DFG latch and an engaged αC tether (Figure 12B,C and Table 1).
evidence: This is based on crystal structure analysis shown in Figure 12B and C.

claim: The four-site allosteric model for FGFR kinases is applicable to other RTKs based on structural similarity.
source: Based on the structural similarity shared among RTKs, we propose that this allosteric model for FGFR kinases is applicable to other RTKs.
evidence: This is a proposal based on structural similarity.

claim: The multi-site mechanism has evolved as a defense mechanism to diminish the detrimental effects of opportunistic mutations.
source: Since the probability of acquired mutations simultaneously occurring at two sites in a cis fashion is extremely low, we propose that this multi-site mechanism has evolved as a defense mechanism to diminish the detrimental effects of opportunistic mutations.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary advantage of the multi-site mechanism.
